utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Monday, August 17th, 2009, and we are resuming with our hearings. I would like to welcome Mr. Praljak, Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Petkovic, and Mr. Pusic. I would not want to forget to also greet Mr. Coric, who's not with us at the moment. I would also like to welcome the counsels. Most of them are here. And I also welcome the representatives of the OTP in this room, Mr. Stringer and Mr. Scott, as well as their assistants. And, of course, I would like to welcome all the people helping us daily; our Court -- our Registrar, our usher, and our interpreters. I would like -- could we please move into closed session for a moment, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In open session, let me greet again Mr. Stringer. Mr. Stringer will resume his cross-examination. I would also like to thank the Prosecution for having provided us with a document where we have all the different topics that are going to be addressed. This document was circulated to everyone, since it was recorded. It's a document that dates to August 10th. And thanks to this document, we'll be able to follow the cross-examination in a much better fashion. Thank you, Mr. Stringer. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President, good afternoon. Good afternoon Your Honours, Counsel, and to everyone else in and around the courtroom. Before I begin, I would like to briefly introduce to the Trial Chamber Ms. Amarys Preuss. She's joined the Office of the Prosecutor recently as a legal intern. She's from France. She's currently studying in Aix-en-Provence, and she may be assisting us in the courtroom in the coming months.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, when we left off with the cross-examination questions last month, we were in documents that relate in general to what we're calling the joint criminal enterprise that's alleged in the indictment. And as a way to re-introduce some of the issues that are involved, what I'd like to do briefly, and I don't think you need to go back to the document because we covered it already at length, it's the presidential transcript which is P00089. You may recall, General, that this was a transcript of a conversation that occurred on the 27th of December, 1991, although you were not present. I was asking you about it, and I'm going to ask you -- actually, I'm going to -- perhaps with the assistance of the booth, we could put it up on e-court so that the general could see the part I'm going to read from, rather than taking the time to go to the page, which is page 98. And on page 98, we see that President Tudjman is speaking, and this is what he says. And after I read this to you, General, I'm going to move on and begin my cross-examination again. Skipping down a paragraph, he says to the group: "All of history has shown that Bosnia and Herzegovina is no solution for the Croatian people. "First of all, gentlemen, let us not forget that it, Bosnia, was created in the colonial conquests of an Asian power, at the expense of the Croatian people and Croatian territories, between the 15th and 18th centuries. "All colonial creations throughout history fell, both in Africa and Asia. Bosnia and Herzegovina did not exist between the two world wars. The Communists invented it, put it back on the map after World War II, even declared the Muslims to be a nation in order to, supposedly, resolve the differences between the Serbian and the Croatian people. "Did they succeed? No, on the contrary. Therefore, Bosnia and Herzegovina should not be taken as something god-given which must be preserved. We must especially not forget how harmful it is. Because of the creation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia has been put in an impossible situation regarding its territory, regarding administration, not to mention defence. We cannot establish an independent Croatia, such as it is." So, General, with that as our starting point, those words of President Tudjman from December of 1991, I want to take you back to one of the exhibits I showed you just before the break which we decided to leave for now so that we could get you the original language version, and that is Exhibit 1D00401. Do you see that? That is an excerpt from a book by President Tudjman from 1991. Now, General, I see you reaching for what appears to be the original text. Is that correct? Have you brought the book here today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it wasn't published in 1991. These texts were written 15 years before. You have the 1991 edition because I think that's when they were translated into English. Otherwise, they were written before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm reading what's on this Defence exhibit, but I'll accept your statement on that. Now, what I want to direct you to, and I'm going to turn, in the English version which we have of this exhibit, it's page 112, but I believe that in the Croatian version it is page 103. So if you could turn to page 103, and we'll see if it corresponds, General, because I might have the Croatian version from a different text. And so if yours doesn't correspond, we'll have to go to my version of it. And I'm going to start reading at the bottom of page 112 of the English, and you see if you can follow me. Tell me if you cannot. Tudjman writes: "Several reasons could be given in favour of the decision to unite Vojvodina with Serbia." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: "The two areas had strong historical, national, economic, and cultural ties, and their union was also in the interest of the state community as a whole. The fixing of the boundaries for Vojvodina and Serbia is a different question and will be discussed later. However, there are many indications that the same logical criteria were not applied in the case of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which, according to the same yard-stick, should have been made a part of the Croatian federal unit." Then he talks about how Bosnia-Herzegovina was established with borders set during the Turkish occupation. He says: "But large parts of Croatia had been incorporated into Bosnia by the Turks. Furthermore, Bosnia and Herzegovina were historically linked with Croatia, and they together comprise an indivisible geographic and economic entity. Bosnia and Herzegovina occupy the central part of this whole, separating southern (Dalmatian) from northern (Panonian) Croatia. The creation of a separate Bosnia and Herzegovina makes the territorial and geographic position of Croatia extremely unnatural in the economic sense and, therefore, in the broadest national-political sense, very unfavorable for life and development, and in the narrower administrative sense unsuitable and disadvantageous." Now, General, what I want to put to you is that these words written by President Tudjman some 20 or more years prior to the conflict in 1993, if what you say is correct, really are no different than the words President Tudjman was repeating here during this meeting in December of 1991. In other words, his views certainly had not changed in respect of the relation between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with you at all, not in the smallest part. You've read all this wrongly, or read into this wrongly. Of course, to read books like that and read excerpts from books like this is impossible. President Tudjman, since 1968 or 1969, thereabouts, when he was called to attend a congress in Slovakia, he would send out texts that he had dealt with throughout his lifetime, and that is the fate of small nations within large ideas, whether they were the Russian empire, Pan-Slavistic aspirations, Austro-Hungary, or whatever, or whether they be Germanic expansionist thoughts and thinking, or Turkish invasions or whatever, but in that respect he always had a crystal-clear political idea and ideals, and they were composed of two parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My question is this: It seems to me, General, that President Tudjman's words, as expressed in the book I've just read, are entirely consistent with the views of Bosnia and Herzegovina that he expresses in meeting in December 1991; isn't that true? In 1991, he says all history has shown that Bosnia and Herzegovina is no solution for the Croatian people. He makes reference to the historical boundaries established during the Ottoman Empire, et cetera. It's really just remarkably consistent, isn't it, with what he wrote in his book some 20 years earlier?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Bosnia and Herzegovina, as it was formed and as it was constructed politically by Serbian thinkers or Muslim thinkers, was not a solution for the Croatian people, and you can see that on the basis of statistical data, the disappearance of the Croatian people from Bosnia and Herzegovina over the centuries, and that's how it was, the way it was constructed. And then you can draw the historical conclusion that the Croatian people today are rapidly disappearing from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is politically quite clear. It is a historical truth, and it means none other than acknowledging that historical truth without territorial pretensions. He's speaking as a historian here, and every sentence here --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think maybe you misunderstood my question, which was whether you would agree with me that the views expressed by President Tudjman in his book are very consistent with the views he was expressing in December of 1991. It would seem to me that his views have not changed and that they remained remarkably consistent over time. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he's not talking about the same things here. President Tudjman, in this excerpt, the one that you were quoting from, stated exactly in what way the national question was being solved in Yugoslavia, either through the Versailles Treaty or the taking over by the Serbs [indiscernible] of territory after their victory in World War I, not only at the expense of the Croatians but of the Hungarians too. There were half a million of them in Banat. There were half a million of the Volksdeutchers in Vojvodina, and the Serbs, under the treaty, were not allowed to move into Vojvodina, which had previously come under the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Anyway, well, if you want an answer, I'm here to give you an answer. And this text is about history, and here we see a fact, that the Croatian people will disappear from Bosnia and Herzegovina if Bosnia-Herzegovina is constructed in the manner it has been constructed today, and that's the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I asked you whether the views appeared to be consistent. You disagreed with me, you said, "No," so I'll take that answer and I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What I'm going to do now -- what I'd like to do now, Mr. President, is go back to some of the video footage that we tried and failed to run in Courtroom I just before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, General, I'm going to take you back to the film of a couple of the interviews that you gave to the BBC when they were making the "Death of Yugoslavia" programme, so let me play these two videos for you, and then I'm going to ask you some questions. So if you want to watch the screen in front of you, you should be able to follow along.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voice-over] "We shall return to this issue later, but now we're here, I would like to talk about -- so, on the one hand, you had a communications problem regarding both political and military cooperation with Izetbegovic and the Muslim Army. On the other hand, however, the leadership in Zagreb fully supported you. How was this support manifested? Can you give us a specific meeting, an action? Can you give us a story? "Well, there were many meetings. The support consisted of -- once it was realised what the intentions were -- well, the problem was that before the war, we were military allies with the Muslims, but had opposing political ideas about a future state. To be honest, the Serbs' political option for Bosnia-Herzegovina was closer to the Croats' view than that of the Muslims. Oneness was out of the question; either we shall amend the Constitution to provide equal rights, or we'll go our separate ways. Now, as soon as there is a lack of trust, you cannot put all -- everything on one card."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right, General. Before we move on to the next one, I want to ask you -- and transitioning now from the views of President Tudjman that were expressed in the various presidential transcripts and his book, and I want to talk now about your views and your objectives in respect of Bosnia-Herzegovina and your involvement down there. You say here that: "To be honest, the Serbs' political option for Bosnia-Herzegovina was closer to Croats than that of the Muslims." It seems to me, General, and I'm going to put this to you, that what you're saying there is that the Serbs' option, which was a separateness, the establishment of autonomous ethnic territories, was closer to the option and the objectives of the Croats, such as yourself, and that this was as part of an effort or a desire to consolidate a Greater Serbia, on the Serb side, and perhaps a Greater Croatia, on the Croatian side. Is that what you're saying when you said that your option was closer to that of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, I cannot agree that in the two texts that we've seen before us, that Mr. Tudjman is talking about two different things which you're claiming. I say that that is not so. And, secondly, it's not a question of any ethnic division and separation within Bosnia and Herzegovina here. And according to you're indictment, ethnic cleansing follows on from that. But there were talks and meetings held in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the very beginning, that is to say, before the war, when the Serbs did not talk about what they were preparing, at least not publicly. So we're talking about the public option, and that is that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be constructed and formed as a community of three constituent peoples, all of them having equal rights. And the main conflict between Izetbegovic and Karadzic, on the other side, was that Izetbegovic from that time on always claimed that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be a civil state, one man, one vote, unitary -- let me -- allow me to finish, please -- unitary, without any protection of national rights, stating in one particular text that it will either be a civil state or there'll be civil war, which is what ultimately happened. And I claim today and I said so then that in that respect, without going into any ethnic questions, it would be a good idea to construct Bosnia-Herzegovina in the sense that it was proposed later on by all the international negotiators, starting with Cutileiro onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about your words here and what you said when you indicated that your option or the Croatian option was closer to what the Serbs wanted. Now, that leads to my next question, which is based on the next thing you said. "Oneness was out of the question," and what you're telling us there, and I think you've said it many times here in a different way, is that this is a rejection of the unitary state model for Bosnia-Herzegovina, the one-man-one-vote model, and then in fact what you and those with you on the Croatian side embraced, like the Serbs, was the establishment of an autonomous unit, an autonomous, separate living space for Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Isn't that what you're saying here when you say "oneness is out of the question"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that unity or singleness, oneness, was never an option. This is quite a different idea from a unitary state that cannot survive and serve all three nations equally well. And Tudjman, in his books, shows this very clearly, that they will --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm asking you now about --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- disappear --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. I'm asking you now about your views. You talked about the views of President Tudjman a great deal in this trial, but I've got you here in the witness box and so I want to talk about your views. And when Slobodan Praljak says to the BBC here that oneness was out of the question, I'm putting to you, sir, that what that means is that you're rejecting the unitary state system of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you are advocating instead a separateness based on autonomy and territory for different peoples. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, that's what I advocated then, I advocate that today, and I think that in Bosnia-Herzegovina a catastrophe was provoked because a nation was given a republic, that nation having committed many evil deeds, and this nation is disappearing slowly. So today I am advocating these interests crystal clear and the fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina should have been established at the beginning in the same way that Switzerland is formed. I don't want Judge Trechsel to be angry with me when I say that. You can't, of course, create a Switzerland in the space of a fortnight. But that was a model for Bosnia-Herzegovina. Unfortunately, that did not happen, and even through the mediation of the international community, what happened was that a system was established which was untenable. So I stand by what I said. I fully support my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's go to the next clip, then, to continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "And this brings me to the basic question of whether we are going to wage war. We were no longer ready to wage a war, and so this unity or dis-unity of Bosnia became absolutely clear and obvious. The option of a state which constitutionally -- well, if we cannot agree about the Constitution, if you want us to be second-class citizens, then we would be prepared to secede militarily."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, that's the next step. You've expressed some agreement with me about -- or you've indicated to us what your view was of how Bosnia and Herzegovina should be configured internally, and here you indicate, I'm putting to you, that you, the HVO, your co-accused, President Tudjman, Gojko Susak, were prepared to exercise a military option in order to create this separate Croatian living space, this separateness, because, as you said, oneness was out of the question, so that military secession, as you refer to it here, is really what the war with the ABiH was all about; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you in very few things, but what you said, that we agree on certain matters, is not correct, unfortunately. Mr. Prosecutor, we agree on basically nothing. Either you do not wish to interpret the problem clearly or you are putting forth the agenda proposed by the indictment. I do not agree with that, and I do not agree with your interpretation of this part. This interview came about after my talks with Mr. Izetbegovic in Mostar in 1992. I have mentioned that. During that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This interview came about after the war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. Yes, the interview, but the ideas I'm expressing in the interviews is simply conveying the discussion I had with Mr. Izetbegovic in 1992 on the topic of the unitary state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And to use a metaphor or comparison, I said that Mr. Izetbegovic, within the domain of his political options, when discussing the unity of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO, proposed a thesis which he often repeated, stating that we need to fight the Serbs, and once we beat them, although it wasn't clear to me how we were supposed to do that, and Mr. Izetbegovic was even more lost on that topic because he kept negotiating with them, it was then that he proposed that we agree on the framework of the state. I asked him, given that death is mentioned, although you omitted that part from your quotation --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I know you've told us previously about this discussion with Mr. Izetbegovic, so I'm going to -- and I'm going to cut you off to try to make it move a little faster here. What you said in the interview here is -- you've said before in this courtroom, essentially, that that was a basic question. Izetbegovic wanted to fight first and agree on the framework later; you and the others wanted to agree on the framework first and then fight on that basis. Isn't that a correct understanding of your testimony on this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I asked to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that people being killed is too dear a price and that we have to have a plan first and then set out to implement it. This is not talking about seceding one part of Bosnia and Herzegovina and annexing it to Croatia. I'm talking here about what I had foreseen, and that is that a conflict would ensue because we did not wish to be ruled by anyone the way we had been ruled throughout history.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the fact is that no agreement with Izetbegovic or the government in Sarajevo was ever reached beforehand; correct? That's a "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, as I'm stating here as well, and you could see that he kept lying, cheating, and breaking every deal, such a deal was not reached. He did consent to one type of agreement -- well, excuse me, but let me finish. We cannot bring this down to a simple "yes" or "no." These are international relations. If you are asking me for an answer, I'm trying to give you as short one as possible. Mr. Izetbegovic did not have a plan at first. The plans he consented to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I asked you whether there was agreement or not. You said that there was not, and we all know that there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When, when? There was an agreement in 1993 by way of the Vance-Owen Plan. He broke that. Then there was another one in early summer --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'll talk about Vance-Owen later and the fact that it never came into being because the three sides never accepted it. It never became operative as an international instrument or treaty. What I'm putting to you, and you're free to disagree with me, and you probably will, but what I'm putting to you, General, is that when you make this statement here in this interview, that, "If we cannot agree about the Constitution, if you want us to be second-class citizens, then we would be prepared to secede militarily," you told that to the BBC interviewer as the statement you made to Izetbegovic, what I'm putting to you is, in fact, the war with ABiH, certainly in the area of Herceg-Bosna, was about just that, it was about the HVO's objective to obtain or to impose its vision, its separate living space, within that Herceg-Bosna territory. That's what the war was ultimately about; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are using a rather strange term, "living space," which in German has a bad -- negative connotation, "lebensraum." I disagree with you. We did not ask for such type of space to live in. We were asking for another thing. We did not want to become second-class citizens in a state we helped create. If someone wanted to subdue us, as the Serbs and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina tried to do so, I said we would fight. I can tell you this: I'm sorry that we have Bosnia and Herzegovina as it is now, and if it were up to me, I would have never signed that. We were simply forced to do so by the forces which directed our fate through centuries. We were supposed to sign something which is unjust, which is beyond reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me take you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. May I be allowed to make a little correction to the transcript. As it is a German term, I don't know whether someone else will be able. It is "lebensraum," not "trama" or the "traum," which would be possible but means something quite different, "lebensraum." And the reference, Mr. Praljak, you made critically is "volk ohne raum." That was one of the key sentences of the Nazis. Would you agree to that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Prosecutor said the Croatians wanted their own "lebensraum" or living space. This is a grave accusation. It is not correct. Correct is what I say. I stand by my words, save for certain interpretations. We did not want to be second-class citizens in our own state. That was key. The right not to be second class is one's natural and just right. That was my position. Unfortunately, another thing happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And there's been testimony in this trial by a number of witnesses, and I believe you've talked about it as well, that over time demographically the percentage or the proportion of Croatian or Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina was diminishing, and it's for that reason that the unitary system or the one-man-one-vote system for you would not work for Bosnia-Herzegovina because Croats or Croatian people could always be out-voted in such a system, correct, assuming that people would always vote along ethnic lines, of course?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is in our interest, national, economical interests. We went through various empires, the Turkish, Austro-Hungarian, Italian, and so on and so forth. It was for such state institutions that there are more Croats as emigres from Australia to the Americas than in the territory covered by Croatia. The percentage of the Croat population was reduced significantly after the agreement after the end of the war for the simple reason, and that was that there are some natural laws in place in a society which can be packaged nicely using skilled words by those who are ignorant of history. In this way, solutions were offered to us which can end in disasters when small nations are concerned. This is precisely what is happening to the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: On the 29th of June, this is what you said about the objectives or the aspirations of those that you were with. You say: "We were hoping --" This is page 42159 of the transcript, line 22: "We were hoping all the time that the leadership would finally understand that Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina wanted only one thing, and that was an autonomy in the area that could have been 17 or 18 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, an area in which they were an absolute or relative majority, equal to anybody else, and that was all; nothing else, only that, and there were also some human connections." Do you recall that testimony? Shall I read it to you again?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall my testimony. Some documents speak about that as well, including certain statements I gave at meetings with the French delegation in Zagreb. We kept repeating that as parrots. That was our natural request. Nothing has changed in the meantime, save for the fact that there are no longer 17 or 18 per cent of us. Even that figure is, historically speaking, incorrect, because many people from Austria and other countries did not come to join the census. This is something that is often taken at face value but may not necessarily be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So now within this autonomous area where Croats were going to have an absolute or a relative majority, was it envisioned that because of their majority, in terms of population, the Croats then would be autonomous in terms of self-governance? They could govern that territory as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, not Croats. In that area, which had after all ultimately been set up since Cutileiro, the rule of civic democracy would be in place. In such a case, the protection of other ethnicities in that area would be a mirror image to the protection Croats who were outside that territory would enjoy. This would ensure protection both ways and would be a precondition for a sensible development of that state, but the way it was set up was not incorrect, and the state as it exists today is untenable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So what you wanted was an autonomous territory within Bosnia-Herzegovina where Croats were an absolute or relative majority, but where there could be protections for minority also living in that territory; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not minorities. These would be equal citizens, not minorities. One cannot have three constituent peoples within a state and that those same peoples would at the same time be minorities. That's impossible. The state should have been constructed in keeping with what the international factors proposed, and that is to say that the state was supposed to be made up of either cantons or republics. That is -- the name is of lesser importance, in which way the national interests of each of the peoples would be protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to ask the Trial Chamber to intervene, I'm trying to get more succinct answers from the general. I think I'm entitled to that. I think he's wasting a lot of time, going far beyond what is needed in terms of his testimony, and so I'm going to ask the Trial Chamber to intervene rather than continuing to argue with him or cut him off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, the Prosecutor is asking you difficult questions, but they are essential questions. So if you are not in agreement with a question asked, say so, say that you're not in agreement with the question. And then if he wants you to complete your answer, he will tell you why, and then you will eventually develop, because the Prosecution has got time and he wants to use the time in the best possible way. So when he feels that you do not answer exactly to his questions, he tries once again to reposition you on the question, and finally he requests the Chamber to tell you this is what should be -- this is the problem. So when you are in a cross-examination stage and you say, "I agree," or, "I don't agree," or, "I don't understand ," if he then wants you to be specific, then he will ask you to be specific. You will have noted that for the last hour or so, I did not intervene. I let things happen normally while the Prosecutor was asking questions his question on this important subject, and therefore I'm letting the Prosecution continue. I may have, myself, questions to ask, but for the moment try and answer precisely to the questions asked from the Prosecution. And if you think the question requires some specifications, tell him. Tell him you disagree or tell him, "I might answer, but I need more time," and you'll see what he wants exactly. So let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pardon me, Mr. Stringer. In the transcript, there is something missing. What is the exhibit number of the video excerpts we saw? I don't think we have that in the transcript. We don't have the number. I cannot follow it, and I was unable to locate it in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel. The first clip was P09447, or it was a part of it. The video, itself, is longer. And then the second clip came out of P09488.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, General, I want to come back again to your testimony about your objective here for an autonomous area, where Croats would be an absolute or relative majority. Would you agree with me that such an area, for it to exist, would have to have an identifiable border?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that such an area that you envisaged, that you're speaking about here, would not be a temporary entity under Bosnia-Herzegovina or within Bosnia-Herzegovina, but that what you wanted was a permanent autonomous area for Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina ?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was supposed to be permanent. We agreed with the international proposals which went along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And would you also agree with me that in order to maintain these Croat -- or to achieve and maintain these absolute or relative Croat majorities, it would be necessary to control, over time, the ethnic composition of that territory?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you understand by controlling the ethnic composition? Can you explain that to me? How do you envisage one controlling an ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I guess that's what I'm asking you. Given the trends that were taking place over the decades, where Croatian people were moving away either to Croatia or elsewhere, Muslim people were moving in from other places, in order to maintain this Croatian autonomous area, perhaps you could tell us, how was it proposed or envisaged that Croatian people would maintain their majorities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing was proposed or envisaged of that type. Such type of control, without going back to certain fascist and Nazi systems, is impossible. The only discussion that occurred was that this would prevent the departure of Croatian people, be it to Germany, France, Switzerland, or Croatia, because they would be able to enjoy their ethnic, national, and civil rights. Since that failed to realise, the situation that we now have in Mostar [as interpreted] is that by now we have the Muslim majority, and this is the result of the lack of comprehension, and that is something that anyone historian could explain to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise to Mr. Stringer. I have a correction at page 25, line 3. General Praljak discussed Sarajevo, rather than Mostar. Is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, but I could have said "Zenica" or any number of cities. This would serve as a protection, preventing people from leaving, which is something that more or less occurred en masse.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I'm going to put it to you that certainly based on the situation that prevailed in 1991 and 1992 and 1993, that in order to achieve this autonomous Croatian area, where Croats would be an absolute or relative majority, what was absolutely required, in terms of controlling the demographics, was to move Muslim people, non-Croats, out of many of these areas in order to tip the balance ethnically back toward Croats. Isn't that true? Isn't that what was necessary?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean remove them the way you did with the Indians? No, we did not have that. Quite the contrary. When Herceg-Bosna was being established and during the fight, in hundreds of examples, as you could see, Croats protected each and every Muslim in that territory. In terms of military-judicial practice, there was no distinction between the two. Please do not interpret it that way and impute that to the Croats. It is incorrect, and I refuse to discuss this along such lines unless you show evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to put it to you directly, General, we're going to be talking about a lot of places like Prozor in October of 1992, Gornji Vakuf, January, the events in Mostar and Western Herzegovina throughout the summer of 1993, where we see hundreds -- thousands of Muslims evicted from their homes, put in camps, driven away. And what I'm putting to you is that that was all part of this need, on your part and the part of your colleagues in the HVO, to establish a Croatian autonomous area where Croatian people would be a majority -- an absolute or relative majority. Isn't that what all these crimes that took place were about, the creation of a Croatian area in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. In Prozor, that was not the case. 90 per cent of the people returned after the incident which was caused by the Muslims. Gornji Vakuf was divided. Mostar, which under that interpretation, was supposed to be the central part of Herceg-Bosna, was split in two. In the Muslim part, there were 140 Croats left, whereas in the Croatian part there were at least 7.000 Bosniaks. Everything you said is not true, and you keep using these empty words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's talk about the Muslim refugees who came into Herceg-Bosna from other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina after they were evicted and driven away by the VRS, the Serb armies. As a starting point, it was going to be imperative --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question to ask, a follow-up question. The Prosecutor asked you a series of questions on the geographical entity which might have been established where Croatians would have had a majority or a relative majority, and while listening to him I wondered whether he wasn't creating a parallel between the Vojvodina, because a moment ago we saw, in the book written by Mr. Tudjman, that there was a whole paragraph concerning the Vojvodina. As you know, Mr. Praljak, since everybody knows about this, this is public knowledge, I can speak about it, Vojvodina is a province -- an autonomous province of Serbia where there would be 25 different ethnic groups, as one reminds me of, and which is -- and six different languages which are used, including Hungarian. Hungarian is one of the languages used in Vojvodina, but Vojvodina is a province which is an autonomous province. Now, do you and your friends and others thought maybe to create in Herceg-Bosna an autonomous province within Bosnia-Herzegovina? Was it a possible assumption, hypothesis, which had been muted, or was the Herceg-Bosna scheme had nothing to do with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was precisely the foundations of our thinking for the establishment of Bosnia-Herzegovina, precisely to create autonomous provinces. You are well-acquainted with the situation, that is to say, in Vojvodina before World War II there were more than half a million Hungarians, half a million of what were known as Volksdeutchers, there were 200.000 Croats in Backa and Srem, those provinces, there were some Jews, and so on and so forth, Romanians, and an autonomous province was established. The Serbs were -- of course, they were in the majority, individually speaking, but I don't think the number exceeded 35 or 36 per cent compared to the total population. So in the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, there were already existing models. Kosovo was in Serbia, too. It was an autonomous province, the autonomous province of Kosovo. Before, there was Sandzak. Sandzak was autonomous during World War II, with an anti-fascist movement, the Sandzak anti-fascist movement, and then was divided up between Serbia and Montenegro, six districts to Serbia, two districts to Montenegro, and the Bay of Kotor as well, which was [indiscernible] since 1918, was part of Bavaria, and during World War II it was a separate area, and so on and so forth. So wherever this principle of autonomy was not respected, but the unitary principle was applied, the minority nation disappeared, and that's the law, that's how things went. After World War I and World War II -- well, after World War II, perhaps the Hungarians fared worse. 1.300.000 of them remained in Slovakia, Transylvania, and I'm sure the Judge -- Judge Prandler will know this better than me. A million and a half in Romania, half a million in Yugoslavia and so on. But, anyway -- and so where the Hungarian people were in the vast majority, these territories of Hungary were clipped, and we see all these post-World War Two examples, migrations of Germans in the Sudetenland, Silesia, and so on. So all the proposals were made to prevent a situation of that kind occurring and to have a logical solution, and there were already logical solutions in the offing, and that was autonomous provinces within Bosnia-Herzegovina, whether they be called cantons or autonomous province or whatever. The name was immaterial. The essential point was that the constitutional order should guarantee each and every nation their rights, without having to move out and relocate. We moved during the Turkish Empire, the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, and during modern-day Yugoslavia, and the number of Croatian emigres amounts to three and a half million of the second, third, and fourth generation, and that's a catastrophe. So, Your Honours, all this is tantamount to just stories put out, intended to pass off normal political thinking as a criminal act. So in that respect, we treated the Muslim people as our equals until the spiral of war escalated and brought terrible things to pass, as is the case in every war, but not at a single moment did anybody that I talked to or I knew -- nobody's thinking went along those lines. The only question was how to prevent what had happened in the past from happening again. But it did happen when we had an "Islamic Declaration Plan" at the basis of a state, and then when this person wanted to make you a second-class citizen. So that was the situation. And we lost in Bosnia and Herzegovina because a very distorted state came into being in Bosnia-Herzegovina, thanks to the American political thinking, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, when we talk about this, just for the record, I should ask you, when we talk about this Croatian -- this autonomous Croatian area that you spoke about in your testimony in June, what we're talking about is the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, correct, which then became the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna? That is what was envisioned to be the autonomous Croatian area that you have been talking about; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Herceg-Bosna was established as a defence organisation. In every portion of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was sufficient numbers of Croats for them to be able to associate and to set up an armed uprising to prevent themselves from being exterminated. But as far as I know, certain parts of Herceg-Bosna were to remain parts of, for example, the autonomous province of the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to go back to my original -- the last question I was going to, which was to take you back to 1991, 1992, and into 1993. You've testified a lot about the so-called ethnic occupation, as I think you put it, where many Muslims came into the Croatian territories from elsewhere, driven out by the Serbs. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in order to achieve this autonomous Croatian area and to achieve the majorities that were envisioned, it would, at the very least, be necessary to move those people back out, send them home, send them elsewhere, but to move them out of this Croatian territory; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis of every setup in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in logical terms, was that first of all the results of the war should be abolished to enable all people to go back to their own homes, and to abolish the effects of ethnic cleansing or the fact that people had left out of fear and so on, to create conditions whereby each person could safely go back. That's a humanistic option which is always repeated again and again, but never actually takes root. Everybody goes home satisfied that they've created another Frankenstein who -- well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Some parts of Herceg-Bosna or some parts of this Croatian territory where the HVO is exerting its authority, its military authority and its political authority, it was also going to be necessary to change the demographic composition among Muslims who were living in these territories for years and generations, such as Jablanica and Stolac; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, completely incorrect. Had we wanted to change the ethnic composition of Stolac, then in 1992 we would not have enabled all the Muslims to return to their homes and to set up their own armed force with my help, to set up a brigade, and to fight together with us, and you've seen documents to that effect here before. So not in our wildest dreams did we wish to do anything to persecute any nation within Bosnia-Herzegovina. What happened in 1993 has completely different causes, and those causes belong to the whole war situation and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then, thirdly, of course, in order to maintain this demographic composition of majority -- absolute or relative majority, it would be helpful as well, wouldn't it, if Croats from other territories and other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina were to come down and live within this autonomous Croatian area that you've talked about, to set it up, and then to have other Croatian people move in? That would assist in maintaining the requisite majorities, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. As far as I know about the plans drawn up by the international community, not a single cantonal line was drawn to have people relocate somewhere or come in somewhere, but on the basis of the 1991 population census and the descriptions thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about plans of the international community. I'm asking you about the goals and the policies of the HVO. And it was, indeed, a goal and a policy of the HVO to bring Croat people from other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina into Herceg-Bosna in order to strengthen those territories as being Croatian territories; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Untrue. That is an insinuation not backed up by any proof or evidence. You're just saying it just like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let me then put this to you: that in order to achieve or to maintain any sort of demographic control, what's likely to result and what may, in fact, be envisioned right from the start is violence, some form of violence, to move people away from places where they are living, and that you knew, and your co-accused knew, and President Tudjman knew, in the meetings that were taking place all the way back, as far back as 1991, that when you were talking about creating an autonomous Croatian area, contrary to the legal-constitutional framework of Bosnia-Herzegovina, this was going to result in violence, violence necessary in order to drive non-Croat populations out; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea what you're talking about. Would you break that up into smaller questions, where the Croatian area was mentioned, who mentioned it first, where the order was given for any population movement and relocation? So unless you ask me specific questions, then I take your questions to be just off the bat, which might have, in your history, American history, might have certain good examples, but not in our part of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General, I'm talking about your words here when you're talking about what you wanted; autonomy in the area, territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where there were absolute or relative majority. Now, in order to achieve that, when you talk about maintaining demographic control, that is always going to result in violence, isn't it, because it's going to result in the prevention of people moving or staying as they wish; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's completely untrue. Tell me, please, in any country -- well, there's migration all over the world; England, America, France. Now, if you're preventing 10 million of your citizens to gain citizens' rights, but you're using them as a labour force, that doesn't mean to say we did that down there. Perhaps you could perform this analysis in America, but we adhered to -- let me finish. We adhered to the stands and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No. Mr. President, there is an argument that's taking place here that's rather one-sided. I'm not going to argue with the general, and I'm not going to accept repeated personal remarks of the kind that are starting to flow in my direction. I'm going to ask the Trial Chamber to take control of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, don't make any personal comments on what might have happened in the US, or in France, in Hungary, or elsewhere. The Prosecutor is asking you questions on Herceg-Bosna. He has a case to put, and he's putting it to you relentlessly. You can agree with it or not. I thought I understood that you really disagree, so tell him, "I disagree," and just let him put his questions. But I do have a follow-up question to ask you. On several occasions, the Prosecutor is saying an absolute majority or relative majority. While listening, I'm wondering about one thing. In Herceg-Bosna, was there a majority or a relative majority of Croats? I'm wondering, and I'm wondering because, thinking about Vojvodina, in this autonomous province of Vojvodina, the Serbs represented 65 per cent of the population, and the Hungarians 14 per cent, so there was a Serbian majority, and still it was an autonomous region, so I would like to know whether Herceg-Bosna could have operated with a majority of Muslims, possibly, but with a strong presence of Croats. When the Prosecutor is putting this question to you, I think that in his mind the majority in Herceg-Bosna was a Croat majority. Do you agree with him or not on this point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Herceg-Bosna did not have the borders that we're talking about, but let's assume that there was some kind of Herceg-Bosna which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I'm asking a very specific question. When you're talking about Herceg-Bosna, I would like to know whether there was a Croat majority in that region, or whether there were maybe 40 per cent of Croats but more Muslims. That's what I'd like to know. In Vojvodina, the Serbs were a majority, they were 62 or 65 per cent of the population. I would like to know whether in Herceg-Bosna there was a Croat majority. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, look at it this way: In 1918, when the Serbs crossed the Danube, there were not more than 35 or 37 per cent of Serbs in Vojvodina, and then they impose that kind of administration and system whereby the Hungarians moved out, half a million Volksdeutchers were sent home, the Croats were sent home, and when they established the autonomous province there was 65 per cent of them. That's what we wanted to avoid. That's what this is all about. So where we were in the majority and the province of Posavina, Odzak, that area and West Herzegovina, there was an absolute Croatian majority there, and it was in this absolute Croatian majority, to the surprise of the Serbs, is the Banovina Hrvatska of Croatia was established. It was established when the Croatian had an absolute majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Prosecutor is asking a second question to you, and you haven't answered it. He put a very simple question to you. He was asking whether you and also those in the HVO, maybe Tudjman and others, didn't have the political will to make sure that this region would be peopled by Croats, you know, with Croats coming from elsewhere in order to increase the number of Croats there. That's what the Prosecutor is asking. Do you agree with him; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, and three times "no." And I say that here and now, and I say that in this text in the interview. I address that issue too. But then we should look at the integral text, and if we have time to do that, well, we have time. If not, we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, you have the floor. So he is answering "no" to the question you put to him, the idea you had that they might have wanted to increase the number of Croats by bringing Croats from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit is -- I'm going to move to is 3D01279, 1279.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We've got the next binder which we meant to distribute before, but this is all continuation of the same topic, Mr. President. Mr. President, maybe now that -- we could take the break. We're approaching the time, and we could make the distribution now and then start with this when we come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's time for the break, anyway. We'll have a 20-minute break, and we'll resume with a new binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit, I think you have it there in front of you, 3D01279. This is one of the issues of "Croatian Soldier" magazine that you talked about during one part of your direct testimony, and I just wanted to use this to introduce the idea that there were other visions within the Croatian people or among Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina of the structure and relationships between the Croats and the Muslims. And I noticed in this article, in this issue, at the very end, the very last page of your version, the original language version, and it's on page 25 of the English, this article, at the very last paragraph, talks about: "The Serbs are doing everything they can to prevent any possibility of living or co-existing with the other two national groups long into the future." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Serbs are doing everything that they can to prevent any possibility of, and so on and so forth, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it continues down and it says -- and for the record, this is from August 28th of 1992. It continues on, and it says: "The Croatian Community is not attempting to take advantage of the war situation to prejudice and impose political solutions to the future organisation of BH. Instead, it is cooperating and participating in the talks sponsored by the European Community, which are based on organising the state into cantons. However, it is interesting that there are attempts to cause rifts within the Croatian political body by forming the HOS/Croatian Defence Force units, who advocate a unified Bosnia and Herzegovina as their goal." And just briefly on this, General, you made a reference at one point during your direct examination to the HOS, and I just wanted to ask quickly on that: Would you agree with me that during this period of time in mid-1992, and perhaps earlier, that there was this HOS which was a militia that was formed with a large number of both Croats and Muslims who were unified within this particular militia called "HOS "?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is that -- was this "HOS" -- this militia called "HOS," was it composed of Croats and Muslims together?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, much as the HVO. However, the HOS was a party force of the Croatian Party of Rights. The basic idea was based on the policy of the independent state of Croatia, including Ante Pavelic's policies, to the effect that Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia together comprise a single state; that is to say, that the Croatian state stretches up to the Drina, not Bosnia, and that Muslims are actually Croats of a different religion. That is the basic political principle of the Croatian Party of Rights which, during the war, organised HOS. Because our policy was completely different, we had serious problems with them. However, Izetbegovic recognised them as long as he needed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in terms of difference in policy, this article here indicates that at least one of the differences in policy is that HOS advocates a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I take it that is different from the vision of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was envisioned by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you are not right, sir. The Croatian Party of Rights at elections received 5 per cent of votes in Croatia. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, they received none. Unfortunately, Davor Gjenero was not precise here. He only put it partially. The unified state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is not correct. For HOS, Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a unitary state, stretching up to the Drina, was supposed to be a single state, treating Muslims as Croats, as of the constitutional assembly in 1921 and the formation of the kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, out of 40 plus deputies, 20 deputies declare themselves Muslims, 1 -- 2 declare themselves Croats. Based on such distorted view of history, they advocated policies without a foundation. Save for that, it also relied heavily on the idea of the NDH or the independent state of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, the document which Mr. Stringer is showing you is important, it's an important document, and I thank Mr. Stringer for showing it to you. When one reads the last paragraph, it seems that there is -- that there are two aspects on the Croatian point of view, one which is the HOS, impersonated by the HOS, and the other one by the rest. The HOS, you say, represents 5 per cent of the voters in Croatia and 0 per cent for Bosnia-Herzegovina. If I have understood what you said, the HOS wanted a state, a unified state, and this unified state would have been Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina in one single state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And the other Croatians, the other -- the HVO, for their part, were following the European Community trend. They wanted to have a Bosnia-Herzegovina organised like a state, but a state constituted or made up with cantons, which means, if I understand the text properly, there should be the Republic of Croatia as a state, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as another state, but within the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina there would be cantons, including the famous 3, 8, and 10, which would, by majority, have a Croatian population. Is this, indeed, what the text says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. And it reads on that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina never manifested any disloyalty to the Bosnia-Herzegovinian state, they were not disloyal to it. They defended its territory, a significant portion of the territory, and its population. It is also stated that we weren't efficient in repelling the aggressor. Then it says that the Croatian Community is not trying to take advantage of the war situation in order to prejudice and impose any political constitutional solutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We cooperated in the negotiations under the auspices of the European Community, which had a plan based on the cantons, including the three you mentioned. According to the census, there were some 60 per cent of Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. I had to interrupt you. This text, which was published on the 28th of August, 1992, I don't know who wrote it, but if one looks at the beginning of the text, where the Serbians are mentioned, I believe I understand that the Serbians have ethnic cleansing as a solution, but this is not the solution of the Croatian Community. Is this what is, indeed, written in this text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour Antonetti.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, if I understand properly, in 1992, in August, there was a text which was a quasi-official text coming -- published in the "Croatian Soldier" where reference is made to ethnic cleansing by the Serbs, but this is condemned by the Croatian -- by the Croats because they say this is not the solution. Do you agree or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was fully our position, and we behaved accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is what I read here, would be saying. You are the one who actually started this. So I'm giving you the floor again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is it true, General, that HOS recognised the legitimacy or the direction of the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo and that this was one aspect that put it at odds with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We recognised their authority as well. HOS was, unfortunately, a party force. Many great guys were among their ranks who wanted to fight, but, politically speaking, that option was not acceptable. And because of that reason, and because one could not afford to have political armies, with a lot of effort on the part of the HVO we managed to dismember HOS, having many of their troops move over to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. The next exhibit is P00524, which is the minutes of a meeting of the National Defence Council on the 26th of September, 1992. General, you were present at the meeting, and you've testified about these minutes already earlier, and --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, excuse me. All of my Croatian pages are empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Turn to page 17.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't have a look at anything because I only have the English texts. Perhaps there is something here. Sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm looking at page 17 of the English text, and, General, for you that should be -- I'll refer to the ERN number. It should be the page with the numbers ending 2856 on the ERN number, 2856. And I'll read you what you said. You're speaking, and you say: "Mr. President, we have open threats in Croatia from all those staffs. They reject any possible talks about Herceg-Bosna or something similar. They do it openly at the tables of the restaurants and secretly in Baska Vode, in Brela ..." I'm going to skip down: "As it seems now, and due to the people settling on the territory from Travnik and below, I'm afraid our chances will be bad at the moment when the war is over. There's been a great change in the ethnic structure. And to solve that with them by war, the civil, international rights, et cetera, and it will be difficult in any form to expel these people from there, and without expelling those people we will not have a majority there." So, General, this goes back to what I was talking to you before the break, about the need to control or to manage the demographic or ethnic structure within the territories that you wanted to be autonomous Croat territory, and here in this meeting what you're doing is saying that an obstacle to that is the fact that you have a lot of refugees, that it will be difficult to expel them, and without expelling them you're not going to have a majority. So I take that to mean, General, that you considered expulsion necessary to the creation of this autonomous Croatian area that you've been talking about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, completely incorrect. I'm only saying here that one cannot use war to change ethnic structure of any part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that is what was taking place, the ethnic structure. We are not talking about expulsions here, and not of the people who were originally there, but who came because of the war and the result of the efforts of the international community. The principle was that war cannot be used to change ethnic structure. This is a fundamental principle of international law, as far as I know. As for the rumours, at the beginning I was referring to the staffs of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Brela and in Baska Voda in Croatia. It was openly discussed that they could not hurt the Serbs, but that the expelled population would colonise the areas where Croats were in majority and Muslims in minority, and would thus gain a half of the state. The basic principle of international talks was what I repeated, and that is that war cannot be used to change ethnic structure. The Serbs used that and proclaimed that as their elementary military goal. It is clearly stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But what you are acknowledging, General, is the fact that the presence of all those Muslims now in these areas does constitute an obstacle to the establishment of a majority Croatian area; isn't that true? At the very least, the demographics were now an obstacle to the establishment of Croatian majority territory in this area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, in that area, without those who were expelled, we did have a majority. Those who were expelled and ethnically cleansed trespassed to others' properties, houses, occupying other peoples' flats, changing the ethnic composition as a result of the war, which is impermissible under international law. I merely said that if the conclusion of the war would be in violation of international law, and if, for example, there is a war between, say, Switzerland and India and there are 15 million Indians in Switzerland as refugees, that would be impermissible, because that would mean the end of the Swiss. This is what I meant by saying that those people had originally been driven away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, Mr. Stringer has asked you a very pertinent question. He tells you, in his question, that the refugees have created a new situation. How are you going to solve the situation? And I am looking at what Mr. Susak says after you. Well, see what he is saying. It's very interesting. He says there are 20.000 refugees in Mostar and that the orders come from Sarajevo in order to create new Muslim brigades, in a way, at Mostar, Capljina, Stolac. Therefore, Mr. Susak says here, "We have 20.000 more Muslims at Mostar." If you add up these 20.000 Muslims with those who are already there, the Croatian majority doesn't exist any more in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You agree. So how did you think you would solve the problem? The Prosecution believes that you were going to solve it by ethnic cleansing. What do you say? How are you going to solve this problem? Because he advocates because of the number of refugees you don't have a Croatian majority anymore.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply said that if this is not resolved and it would take place after that, we would have the violation of international or domestic law and it would be very difficult to drive those people away. If you allow violations of law and international law, and if you allow a people to occupy you, then there is no solution, there is no rule of law anymore, and you lose a state. The solution is international law, which was supposed to be used to stop the war and bring about peace by just means. That means allowing everyone to go back to where they hailed from. Otherwise, what would take place is what, indeed, did take place, because the 200.000 Croats from Republika Srpska are no longer there. This was an unjust war with an unjust end, and I am sitting here accused of producing that although I spoke out against it. That is why we spoke against it. We said to international negotiators, let us try and grasp the problem at the outset but no one could understand it. The powerful ones devise a solution and, after all that, they look to find someone to blame for the solution. Well, I'm not to be blamed for that. I foresaw this back in 1991, I spoke about that, and all of a sudden now it seems I'm guilty. Well, fine. We were unable to resolve the problem, we knew that, and we did take them in. We constructed roads, we brought food, and we never expelled anyone. After that, the war brought about certain changes in movements because it could not be stopped, but that was not because of our political or military attitude and position. We only defended ourselves, although within the framework of international talks we were always on the losing end, irrespective of the fact that we signed everything. The only thing that matters is force and the stronger side, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next part I want to take you to is found on page 23 of the English, which in your version is the page ending with the numbers 2888. Now, General, in this part of the transcript, President Tudjman is talking. He's talking about his discussions with Mr. Eagleburger, also Vance and Owen, and then there's discussion of a board on which yourself and General Bobetko would participate. And then Tudjman says, in the middle of page 23: "We will openly tell Izetbegovic, when he comes here, what we said in the beginning. There can be no discussion about them establishing military and civilian government in areas that used to be within the Croatian Banovina." Now, General, I'm going to put it to you that President Tudjman is saying that because, in fact, those areas are supposed to fall within this autonomous Croatian territory that we've been talking about so far today, which was itself based upon re-establishment of the Croatian Banovina; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not, sir. Banovina Hrvatska encompassed the whole of Croatia, et cetera. What is discussed here are the areas of Vanja [phoen] and Hrvatska which were in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and such areas were formed because of the absolute Croatian majority. He's only saying here that we should tell Izetbegovic not to use force as he did in Mostar and Rama in order to establish his Muslim authority, but that he should stick to -- well, Sancevic was Croatian ambassador to Bosnia- Herzegovina. Again, what was discussed was that we should establish something that would be able to exist and function as the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, rather than by means of force either by the Serbs or Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, what's being said here is that the president of Croatia is deciding that the president or the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina isn't going to have a say in what authorities are established within these areas; isn't that true? What business is it of Tudjman? It's not his country.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what the behaviour of Mr. Eagleburger and the international community was. If he's still alive, you should call him up, you should bring him here, as well as Messrs. Vance and Owen. Throughout the negotiations, they honoured Franjo Tudjman as a person of influence and authority. Prlic and Boban and others will decide on the fate of their peoples, but they saw Tudjman as a partner. Eagleburger did not tell him, "Well, you have nothing to do with this." Unfortunately, this difficult process lasted for years and Franjo Tudjman's role was actively asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In September of 1992, when this discussion is taking place, in fact, the military and civilian government, certainly the civilian government, in areas located within Bosnia-Herzegovina under the constitutional framework, is going to be a war presidency, since a decree on a state of war has been declared; isn't that true? Isn't there already a framework in place for the establishment of a legitimate civilian government within Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that you could consider it that way, and this civilian authority was set up on the basis of the elections. Authorities were formed on the basis of the results of the elections and not as is done in Western democracies, whereby the winner decides all. In the HZ-HB, the parties became part of the government in relation to the election results. Regardless of the fact that the HDZ was the winner and could have filled all the seats, the government was set up together with the SDA proportionately to the number of votes. This was the case in Rama, Mostar, and so on and so forth, so a more democratic base.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. The Judges have a few questions to ask. Judge Prandler first and then I will have a few questions. Judge Prandler, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to go back to a few pages here, and in order not to forget it, actually, the same transcript, page 17, 17 of 71, and 18 of 71. Here you, Mr. Praljak, you speak about the questions of the refugees, and then I would quote that: "There were some talks in the government that the refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina should be allowed to enter Croatia in any way and at any price, since these refugees are already on the territory where the Croatian people are." And then you continued: "Then from Croatia, under the pressure of the international community, they should be sent to the border and to hell with them." And now my first question is that: It was your idea to send them to the hell, to put it in a way rough -- in a way rather roughly, and because then you continued later on that there has been a great change in the ethnic structure, and on the next page, that is, 18, you continued that: "... and it will be difficult in any form to expel those people from there, and without expelling those people we will not have a majority there." And I repeat again "and without expelling those people we will not have a majority there." So my question is: If it was your view at that time that those people, I mean refugees, should be sent to other countries, and what solutions or forms of solution would you have preferred that very time when the discussion took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Prandler, Your Honour, I never said that they should go to hell. I don't know what the translation of that was, but that's not what I said. I said that they should be placed at the borders and send them where they see fit to go. It's not a good translation. Now, I'm going to state my position, which is this and was always this: When Croatia had over 500.000 refugees, occupied as it was, it was my position that the refugees should be sent to the borders, towards Slovenia and so on, and then in the way -- in a humane way, because we couldn't take them in anymore, that they should be sent out to Europe, and that is because I claimed then, as I do now, because, you see, it's a big problem, even for large countries such as Germany, France, and so on, when such a large number of refugees arrives, then those countries would be more included in a just solution to the Bosnian crisis. That was my position. And, Your Honour, you were able to see what happened when Hungary was faced with a large number of refugees, and Hungary asked that they be taken back.
