But when this problem broke out, nobody minded whether it was a burden or not, how much it cost or didn't, and how it would all end, so I thought that this should be solved in the following way: to show these other countries what the problems were so that the problem could be solved. And I didn't say, "Let them go to hell." That's a wrong interpretation, completely wrong, not the right translation. So it might have been -- I might have said it in a rather blatant fashion, but the fact remains that unless the question of ethnic occupation is resolved, then we've got nothing to discuss. We have somebody waging a war with a view to changing the population structure, and then, of course, it is the political and moral -- and it will be a political and moral catastrophe, and that's what happened to us. And our conduct and behaviour toward refugees is the kind that I've already explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, General Praljak. Then it would be enough for me, as far as your answer is concerned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to say the following: Yes, the translation is quite incorrect. The end part of that text in English on page 17 of 71, where it says "then from Croatia under the -- [In English] "... the community, they should be sent to the border and to hell with them," [Interpretation] nowhere in the Croatian version do you have that. In the Croatian version, it says that under pressure from the international community, they should be placed at the border, and send them to wherever they want to go. Allow them to come into Croatia, and then under pressure from the international community, to be placed at the borders and let them fend for themselves and go where they like. Precisely like the general just said. And there is another problem. Some pages of this document have been admitted into evidence. Now, according to the e-court versions, it is the English pages, that is to say, the translations, that have been exhibited, whereas the Croatian pages are in complete disarray. The pages numbers aren't correct, and General Praljak's experience, that part, continues ten pages later. So the Croatian pages have been mixed up. So we should look through that exhibit once again and see which pages have been admitted into evidence, and to deal with the translation mistakes as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I had a question on pages 22 and 23. Earlier, the Prosecutor was telling you in his question -- he was asking you why President Tudjman decided to get involved in what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and quickly you answered by saying because he was asked to do so, and then you continued speaking about something else. I was listening to you, and I was wondering the following. What you just said is very important. If Mr. Tudjman is looking into what is happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it's not because he wants to recreate this banovina. It may be because he was asked to take care of it, which is what you said. So here's my question. It's quite simple. What evidence do you have to back this, to say that Mr. Tudjman was looking into what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina because the international community had asked him to do so and to play a role in this? Do you have any evidence to back this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. Well, look at the beginning. Why would Eagleburger and Vance-Owen talk so many times, why would they invite him to Geneva sessions, however many there were. Why, if they did not recognise the HZ-HB [realtime transcript read in error "HDZ"] did they invite Mate Boban as an equal participant in negotiations about the internal establishment of Bosnia-Herzegovina, together with Alija Izetbegovic? Had Franjo Tudjman wanted to -- well, why did he need Ambassador Stancevic, the ambassador of the Republic of -- the ambassador of the Republic of Croatia, to Bosnia-Herzegovina? Why do the British and French ambassadors go to visit Franjo Tudjman? Because they're seeking him out, wanting to know his opinions and position. And, of course, Mate Boban and the others down there will either sign or not sign the document. He can make his suggestions and proposals, and he recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina and Sancevic down there, and then he negotiates just like hundreds of other people with their mostly very stupid proposals, and here we have how this all ended.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. I'd just like to put right an error in the transcript. On page 52, line 8, the general said "if they did not recognise the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, why then did they invite Mate Boban to the negotiations?" In the transcript, it says the HDZ and not the HZ-HB, so it should read "HZ-HB."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At all negotiations from the very beginning, that is to say, before Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised from the Cutileiro plan -- well, we've gone through all this. The Croats were always the first to sign. They did not question the existence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and asked for a minimum of political and moral correctness for a constituent peoples to be placed in a position of equality. I think that is so clear and we've said it so many times here that I don't know what else we can add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. General Praljak, in a nutshell, if I understand you correctly, Mr. Tudjman insisted on the interior affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina because, according to you, he had been asked to do so by the international community in order to find a solution to the situation. Is this what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, precisely that. They asked him for that, he made his proposals, but his political options was this: Croatia has recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina, you have an ambassador. However, if they're asking a board to be set up, and the board is something that the international community is calling for, made up of the Croats, then he says Bobetko and Praljak, as far as military issues are concerned, and we're going to send a politician. So this is what Croatia is offering down there, to help them find a solution, and that, of course, fell through as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, in fact, the reason why -- or if the international community sought out President Tudjman's assistance or participation, it's because they knew that he, as the president of Croatia, was the person who was dictating policy within the HZ-HB, that Mate Boban was a puppet, essentially, and that in all matters of substance, particularly involving international negotiations, it would be Tudjman who would ultimately be making decisions on behalf of the HVO and HZ-HB. Isn't that how it really was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Had you shown the clip to the end, you would have seen that I say -- at one point I inform Franjo Tudjman that we would cross the Neretva River. So if what you claim is true, then I couldn't have informed him of that, and I informed him. I said I was going, and you, Mr. Tudjman, can do what you will with it later on, et cetera. So Herceg-Bosna, in the political sense, and Mate Boban as the number-one man, if you will there, was autonomous. It is true and correct that Franjo Tudjman did take into consideration, and this was his constitutional duty, to look into Croatian interests, and we from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'm talking about a double role here, that we very often gave way because the international community managed to persuade Franjo Tudjman, and I explained this in the text where we -- Croatian integralists did not want to see a Croatian state not be established, so we gave way, but it wasn't a just thing or a moral thing to do, to give way. But power is might, of course, might is power.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If you would turn, please, to page 54 of the English. For you, General, it's page 2865 of the transcript P00524. We're going to come back to the HOS for a few moments. General, at this part of the discussion, Gojko Susak is talking, there's discussion about the gentleman named Ante Prkacin, and I believe that you mentioned him once or twice in your direct testimony in connection with a unit that was brought in, attempting to get to Jajce in October of 1992. Is that the same man?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, the same man.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And they're talking about Prkacin being in Zagreb, and wearing a Croatian uniform, and the rank that he was representing himself to hold, and President Tudjman says: "Feel free to send military police to him, if he has got one, feel free to take it away from him." And they're upset about him -- his conduct in connection with wearing the uniform. And then turning to the next page, you say this, General. You say: "Mr. President, please, I would like to say that it is not so simple. Openly speaking, we have used Mr. Prkacin, I personally and in cooperation with others, for destruction of the HOS down there. He has done a good job down there." And the president asks then: "What is he, a major general?" And you say: "Nobody speaks about that whatsoever, nobody has said that. That is how he calls himself. He was allegedly offered a major general rank by Alija Izetbegovic, who invited him up there." And you continue: "However, when we needed him and all of his troops, he was fully available to do whatever was required. On the other hand, we can also say it here, although it was repeated ten times, the HOS issue has been solved just now in Zagreb ..." Now, General, when you said here that you personally, and in cooperation with others, used Mr. Prkacin for the destruction of HOS, what are you -- what are you referring to there? What did you do to destroy HOS down in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What they mean is that the HOS was an irregular party army and that, for example, if somebody were to do something within the HVO and you punish him, then he would take his rifle, report to HOS and place himself under the protection of another army, or if he were to have committed theft or something like that, he would go to HOS. That couldn't be tolerated, of course, at the beginning of the war, and this impossible situation --well, it was difficult to maintain law and order anyway, and with two armies, of which one had its political leader and you didn't know who it was responsible to, and no organ of Herceg-Bosna could do nothing about it, then Mr. Prkacin went down there at my request, and the request of others, and he was shown that there would be an even bigger catastrophe. And as he was a reasonable man, he accepted that and the problem was solved. And now here, as far as Croatia is concerned, that is to say --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. I want to ask you about the HOS events in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The commander of HOS, up until shortly before this meeting, which occurred on September 26th, 1992, the commander of HOS down in Bosnia-Herzegovina was a man named Blaz Kraljevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it's true, isn't is it, General, that about six weeks before this conversation took place at the Presidential Palace, Blaz Kraljevic was assassinated, he was shot to death with others in his car, in the Mostar area in August of 1992; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word "killed," well, you could -- or "assassinated," you can only use words like that when the investigation has been completed. It is true that he died. Whether he was killed, assassinated, or what, I wouldn't go into that until the investigation is finished, and we'll here what the law courts have to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General, you know exactly what happened down there, don't you? He was ambushed and shot to death; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not true. I don't know enough about it to be able to say, and I don't think you do either. And the court investigation is still underway, and we'll have to wait to see what the findings are. Everything else would be speculation, which I don't want to enter into.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the end of Blaz Kraljevic was, in fact, the end of HOS? The destruction of Blaz Kraljevic was, in fact, the destruction of HOS; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the contrary. The situation deteriorated somewhat and it required a great deal of effort to deal with the situation, because there were various rumours going 'round, stories going 'round, so what was needed was a calm end to the situation, whatever it was and whatever had caused it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, when you say that you used Mr. Prkacin for the destruction of HOS, what did you have him do?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prkacin was an independent person, and regardless of the fact that it says here that they used or "you used Mr. Prkacin," well, we talked to him frankly, we asked him to go down and take a look at the situation for himself, which was an impossible situation of two armies on the ground, and that if he arrives at the conclusion that I suggested to him by quoting examples, and if he came to see that my positions were the right ones, not only mine by Boban's and the others, that he could then help solve the situation. And he did help in that respect. I don't think you can use the term "to use Prkacin," that's the wrong word, but in talks like this the wrong words are very often uttered. Well, not very wrong, not terribly wrong, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The assassination of Blaz Kraljevic was very much in the interests of the HVO at that time; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with the word "killing" or "murder." Once again, the investigation is underway. So until we know the facts, I cannot accept the fact that killings or murders would be in anybody's interest. Yes, it would be in everybody's interests to resolve the situation, but I cannot accept that the HDZ was the kind of organisation which would settle matters through killings and murder, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The death of Blaz Kraljevic was very much in the interests of the HVO; isn't that true? General, tell us if you want to take a break.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, we can continue. No, I can't agree with your interpretation. Mr. Blaz Kraljevic was an emigre from Australia. He had a history behind him, a strange history and a strange past, and I did clash with Mr. Blaz Kraljevic in Capljina. That was quite open and clear. I said there couldn't be two commanders on the territory in which I was, so we had this difference of opinion. I had my very set, definite views. But your insinuations about a killing and a murder as the end of it all, that's not true. Not many of his members were deluded -- well, he paraded in his uniform and went 'round collecting some very good guys, but there were also some bad guys who were engaged in some inadmissible activities, but who nevertheless had military protection. And that's the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, well -- hold on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But there were first-class guys, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: After Blaz Kraljevic died, many of the HOS soldiers then actually came over and joined the HVO; isn't that true? The HVO was stronger by virtue of the fact that the HOS was destroyed; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even before Blaz Kraljevic's death, many people who had been in HOS joined up with the HVO, and I talked to them, and I had individual talks and group talks. Cano Stanak [phoen] was a case in point, a brilliant fighter who came over to the HVO. HOS had all sorts. There was some very good and brilliant guys who wanted to lay down their lives for the truth and for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then there were others that Blaz Kraljevic or some people around him had collected. And luckily the situation ended on a positive note, except for the fact that the BH Army gave Prkacin -- well, it was in their interests to weaken the HVO through HOS, but they took some units over and they treated HOS as part of their defence force, which we no longer did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit related to this topic is P10983. This is an article from a publication called "Borba," from the 8th of September, 1992, and it's talking about this issue of the death of Blaz Kraljevic. Page 2 of the English says: "But at precisely the time --" This is about a quarter of the way down from the top: "But at precisely the time when Major General Blaz Kraljevic, whose fighting name is 'Arrow,' was killed on 9 August in Kresevo, near Mostar. News about the conflict between the HVO and the Muslim units, but also between the HVO and HOS/Croatian Defence Forces, began to break through what amounted to a news blockade. HOS units, it was reported at the time, had been recognising the legitimacy and legality of the civil authorities and military commands in Sarajevo, while HVO units did not want to do that." And it skips down and says: "The very day before his murder, which many in Herceg-Bosna blamed directly on the HVO, Kraljevic declared, for instance, that the Croatian Defence Council was solely to blame for the conflicts between Muslims and the HVO and Travnik. 'We are fighting for a state which will be free. It is not important whether the borders are on the Drina, a little bit this way, or a little bit that way. Everything depends on the will of the Croatian and Muslim people who live here. And from the time of Starcevic to this day, it has been clear to everyone who has any knowledge of Croatian history that the Croatian Rights Party has always been a party of the Muslims and Catholics.'" And he continues on. It says: "The very day after Kraljevic was riddled with bullets, his deputy, Colonel Ivica Primorac, transferred from the ranks of the HOS into the ranks of the HVO." Now, let me take you to the next document and then we can talk about these two, because they're somewhat similar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to my learned friend Mr. Stringer and to His Honours. The document Mr. Stringer just read out, document P10983, is not in e-court. My other intervention has to do with this: It is a new document. Since the Bench adopted certain rules on the ability to introduce new documents during cross-examination, when the Prosecutor is examining, then Mr. Stringer should stipulate what this document is about and to what aspect of the indictment it is related to.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question. Given the nature of the questions put to Mr. Praljak, does this mean that the Prosecutor, although it is not stated in the indictment, does the Prosecutor see Mr. Praljak as the person responsible for the death of Blaz Kraljevic? Does this amount to an extension to the indictment? Because it is not currently in it. We were not notified in time that such a thesis about the responsibility of Mr. Praljak would be put forth. This is what we conclude on the basis of the questions that were put to him concerning the murder. I would kindly ask the Prosecutor why he is asking these questions. Otherwise, I would deem this a speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, in response to Ms. Alaburic's remarks, the document, I'm told, is in e-court, or it is now. It's one of the newer ones that we added just within the last couple of days, but I'm told that it is there. And if we -- if we tender the document after the completion of General Praljak's testimony, then at that time we'll do what we always do, which is indicate for what purpose it's being tendered into evidence. And then in response to the remarks from Ms. Pinter, I've gone into this as part of the JCE part of our cross. We have General Praljak's words at the National Defence Council meeting, where he says that he used Prkacin to destroy HOS. The Prosecution's not prepared to make any more specific allegation than that. However, it's extremely pertinent, in our view, to the issue of the joint criminal enterprise, the destruction of a unit that, in fact, had an allegiance to Bosnia-Herzegovina, which in our position is not the -- was not the policy of the HVO. So we're not expanding the indictment. It's our position that all of this goes directly to the existence of JCE, furtherance of the objectives, and the general's involvement in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, I wanted to share something with you and my learned friend. That right at the moment as we were exchanging our views, this document was introduced into e-court. Therefore, my first objection is no longer important, since the situation has now changed. As for the other part, I would like to draw the attention to this Bench's decision pertaining to the intention to use new evidence and documents. If we violate that, we would declare that guide-line null and void. If we allow the introduction of new documents, irrespective of whether they meet the criteria put forth by the Bench or not, then the bottom line might be that it is completely irrelevant in admitting this document. We would end up with an examination which would be based solely on such documents, and indirectly such a document could become evidence. If the Bench recalls the contents of that decision, I believe there is no question about the Prosecutor's obligation by which he has to notify in advance on the intention to use such documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... the new document. You didn't indicate this. Is there a reason to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We don't have to, Mr. President. We're free to use any document that we wish on cross-examination. Now, whether we tender it into evidence remains to be seen. If we tender it into evidence, we will, in conformity with the decision, indicate whether it's something that is tendered for culpability or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, wait, wait, Mr. Stringer. The Chamber made a decision about new documents, where it was said -- I'm not going to -- I don't have the text now in front of me, but it was said that when, during a cross-examination, a new document was introduced, it could be only used to test the reliability of a witness. Now, here it's not on the reliability of the witness, it is on the joint criminal enterprise, this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, his testimony goes -- on this point goes to the joint criminal enterprise, and the testimony obviously is evidence. The topic, in our view, is highly relevant to the existence of joint criminal enterprise. Now, General Praljak said this in a meeting with General Tudjman, that he was involved with or he used Prkacin to destroy HOS. We know what the position of HOS and Blaz Kraljevic was. The general denied knowing whether Kraljevic was murdered, or killed, or how he died. This document was put there on the assumption that he would claim that he wouldn't know, even though it's our submission that he does know very well what happened, and that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, I have heard my learned friend's eloquent, as always, response to the objection that's been put forward regarding the death of Blaz Kraljevic. I do note that the Prosecution, with the greatest of respect, seems to back off somewhat when they say that they are not willing -- they're not prepared to make any more specific allegation than they have done. But, Your Honours, when you review the transcripts and have in mind the focus of my learned friend's questions, it at least appeared patently obvious to me that my learned friend was making an allegation that General Praljak, in some way, shape, or form, was in the know, if not ordered, he knew about the killing of that individual. My learned friend has said but a moment ago that they believe that General Praljak knows more than he says. Your Honours, it's not for the Prosecution, in the discharge of their onerous obligation, to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, to seek to do so by innuendo or by leaving a whiff of suspicion. If they have evidence, they should put it forward. If they do not have evidence, the allegation should not be made. Now, that is my respectful submission. My learned friends, like the Defence, have on numerous occasions lamented the lack of time available to the parties, and spending the amount of time we've spent on this issue, given General Praljak's answer, unless there is clear evidence that they've put -- they wish to put to controvert General Praljak's denial of any involvement in that, we should move on. That's my respectful submission, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I've been extremely cautious on this. The general said it in the meeting. It's the general that said, "I used Prkacin for the destruction of HOS."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't say "I did." It reads "we used."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not going to argue with the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a misquotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The general said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let Mr. Stringer say what he wants to say, Mr. Praljak. You shouldn't interrupt Mr. Stringer, General. Right, Mr. Stringer, would you please conclude what you wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I read to the general his words. He says: "I would like to say that it is not so simple. Openly speaking, we have used Mr. Prkacin, I personally and in cooperation with others, for destruction of the HOS forces down there." Now, I asked the general to tell us how did he use Mr. Prkacin, which was fair. I -- I'm not shy about putting our case to the general, and if I wanted to put to him that he was responsible for murdering Kraljevic, I would have done it. But I was careful about reading the text of what he said, giving the general an opportunity to explain exactly what he meant when he said it. For us, it's not -- it doesn't matter who killed Kraljevic. What matters to the Prosecution on this is that in the Presidential Palace, a major general of the Croatian Army, a member of the National Defence Council, is telling the president of Croatia that he used others for the destruction of HOS, and I'm putting it to him that the destruction of HOS was based upon different policies of HOS and its leadership and the fact that it was in the interests of the HVO. So I don't care whether the general's involved or not in the murder of Blaz Kraljevic. I'm interested in his role in the destruction of HOS, and I've been very careful, I believe, about limiting it to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, I have to go back to the objection of my learned friend Ms. Nika Pinter. This is a new charge, one way or another. The Prosecutor puts it crystal clear, this is relevant for the existence of the JCE. General Praljak mentioned what he did on the record about HOS and Blaz Kraljevic, and the Prosecution is now using that to connect that to the JCE. Your Honours, just think about that. If that story about the death of Blaz Kraljevic is so important for the existence or assessment of existence of the JCE, then in any case it should have been mentioned in the indictment. Another important thing. This Defence, in its possession, has a number of documents about Blaz Kraljevic, about his death, including different reports about his death, different rumours, et cetera. When we were preparing the 68 ter list -- sorry, 65 ter list, we didn't find it necessary to include them on the list. Why would we? No one was charged with the death or the killing of Blaz Kraljevic. In no case it can be important for the existence of the JCE or any other charge. Therefore, this story is irrelevant. General Praljak may answer any question. We will not oppose that. But this has nothing to do with anything. This is merely wasting time. Since the Prosecutor seems to be operating on the basis of certain rumours, as I can tell you, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, where we worked a lot, we know for at least -- at least, and it seems I'm testifying, of at least 30 rumours about the reasons and the way Blaz Kraljevic was killed. It changes from village to village, from one social circle to another. You hear different theories, as General Praljak said. Officially, the judicial investigation was not completed. No one can say for certain how Blaz Kraljevic was killed. Therefore, this is just speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... to us why he asked this question. Now, Mr. Praljak, you told us that you would answer every question. Mr. Stringer tells you, in front of Mr. Tudjman, you said that you had used Mr. Blaz Kraljevic to destroy the HOS -- no, Mr. Prkacin, Prkacin, to destroy the HOS, and Mr. Stringer would like to know about this destruction. What was the reason for it? This is the merit of the question. We're not talking about the murder of Mr. Blaz Kraljevic. What the Prosecution wishes to know, and the Chamber also wishes to know, is why you wanted to destroy the HOS, because this, in front of Mr. Tudjman, you don't explain. So please tell us why you used Mr. Prkacin to destroy the HOS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat. The word used is what's in the text, but it actually means this: Prkacin at that time, or thereabouts, commanded HOS for both Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. HOS existed in Croatia as well as an army. And if you see, therein I say only recently did the Croatian state manage to break up HOS in Croatia, because they had their headquarters, their generals, and units. Hence, the Croatian state was too weak to keep up two armed forces, because at that point the HV was in its inception. Secondly, Prkacin was the military boss of HOS for both states. He cannot be used. He can only be convinced. This number-two man, Mr. Ivica Primorac, was the second person in HOS in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He realised that what was going on in that organisation, in addition to the fighting. When they realised what we had, and that is to say that the existence of two armed forces would only result in an increase in crime and further divisions, and the absolute inability to conduct a unified struggle, they concluded that HOS should simply disappear or, rather, transfer to the HVO. Your Honours, on the one hand we have the accusation that Franjo Tudjman, in his political ideas, saw Bosnia-Herzegovina as part of Croatian territory, and then we opposed HOS and the political party which saw Bosnia-Herzegovina as a single state with Croatia stretching all the way to the Drina with no Serbs in it. Their political option is a state without Serbs. That was the NDH policy, Ante Pavelic's policy. All of us who thought about -- along political lines, this idea gave creeps. This person came from Australia, started doing something which at such turbulent times could result in a disaster. I have nothing to do with his fate, but I intensively cooperated with the second person in HOS, Ivica Primorac, and with Prkacin, with their best commander, Primorac. I talked to them so that they would see where all this was taking us, in terms of organisation and setting up the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HZ-HB. I am very proud that we succeeded in this. I wasn't in it alone. Boban worked on it as well, as well as many others. Otherwise, it would have been a disaster. Two armed forces? We barely managed to assemble one, and we had a minimum of control over the situation, and then someone else pops up, having no authority over most of its soldiers, just popping up all over the place after certain operations, and even having the camp for Serbs in Dretelj which I managed to disband by means of force, a rifle against rifle. Sir, I positioned anti-aircraft machine-guns to open fire if they refused. They had their own camp. Come on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a break, Your Honours? We are almost at the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We are going to take a 20-minutes break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Stringer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm going to move on to the next topic, General, or the next exhibit, I should say, and show you a videotape, part of which we saw during your direct testimony. You played a part of the speech that you gave in Zenica in December of 1992, and I'd like to show more of that video and ask you some questions about it. This is P00842, it's in Sanction, and I'm going to let it play for longer than probably normal for videos, and there are going to be some parts that I'm going to ask that we skip over, but I'm just going to let this roll, Mr. President, if that's okay, and then I may stop at certain points with questions. But it's going to take a couple minutes -- a few minutes, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me actually -- and before we start, General, do you recall the speech that I'm referring to now, the speech you gave in Zenica in December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, partially, yes. I know the basics of what I said, the essential points.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'll show it. It's the one that you -- you showed it to us. You were telling the soldiers not to smoke cigarettes during the time of the ceremony. That's the incident I'm talking about, and so we'll play that now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "At the ready for the homeland, at the ready. "I'm going to inform you with our guests today, and they are the vice-president of the Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Dario Kordic, General Praljak, General Ante Prkacin; the operations zone commander, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic; the secretary of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Ignjac Kostroman; the president of the Zenica Croatian Defence Council, Mr. Dominik Sakic; the president of the HDZ, Josip Pojavnik; the Croatian Defence Council vice-president, Zvonko Popovic; Veronika Malbasic; and the president of the Bureau for Defence, Jozo Jerkic."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Just before we continue, General, a few questions. He's going to speak later, but the General Prkacin that's introduced at the beginning, is that the Prkacin that we've already been talking about today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the flags that have been shown there, and there is one on top of the structure that's behind the speakers, are those Croatian flags, that is to say, flags of the Republic of Croatia, or some --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- variation of the Croatian flag, or what flag is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the flag of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's not the flag of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is it the flag of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that any decree proclaimed it as such, that the -- the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, didn't proclaim it that. It didn't want to have a hymn or flag. It was a flag of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, quite simply, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then the song that was just playing, was that the national anthem of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the Croatian national anthem, but also the anthem of the Croatian people, and Croats in America sing it when there's a festivity, and Australia, or wherever. So it is also the Croatian national anthem in Croatia, but it's much broader than that. It's the national anthem of the Croatian people, wherever they may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We can continue now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I swear to discharge my duties as a member of the Croatian Defence Council with honour and loyalty, and that I will observe conscientiously and responsibly the official orders and commands. I swear on my life to protect and defend my homeland, Herceg-Bosna, its right to exist, and all its citizens. "Fellow soldiers --"

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, what we've heard is the swearing in, and they talk about this more later, but is this the swearing in for members of the Jure Francetic Brigade in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So this was a brigade that fell under the command of General Tihomir Blaskic, or Colonel Blaskic at the time there, who was the head of the -- or commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, if a Muslim person wanted to join this brigade to fight, would the Muslim person have to swear his loyalty to his homeland of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether there were any Muslims there, but there were a lot of Muslims in the HVO. It was a temporary oath and pledge for Herceg-Bosna. I see nothing bad in that. You could either keep quiet or say it out loud.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And Jure Francetic was actually a Ustasha -- a well-known Ustasha commander of the World War II era; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of an Ustasha formation on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a professional unit, not the political section. As far as I know, that was who Jure Francetic was. He died, I think, in 1943. He was killed when his plane was shot down somewhere in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the man who administered the oath to the soldiers just there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember. Probably I know who he was, but not from looking at it from here. I could, I suppose, remember if I were to be shown a photograph or whatever, but not just like this off the bat.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Fellow soldiers, non-commissioned officers, and officers, I congratulate you on completing your swearing-in ceremony. "Thank you. "Jure Francetic, a Croatian Knight, fought alongside the Serbs at the Salonika front. In World War II, he defended the Croatian and Muslim peoples. He expelled the Chetniks from Sarajevo from Mount Romanija and the left banks of the Drina River. We, as his followers, don't want anything more. We believe this to be the Muslim army's objective, too, because only together are we able to stand up to the bloody plans of the Chetniks. On this occasion, I would like to wish you all a Merry Christmas and a blessed New Year 1993, with the wish that we celebrate the next holidays in peace and freedom, because we owe it to our homeland Herceg-Bosna. I would like to ask the commander of the Central Bosnia 3rd Operations Zone, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, to take the floor. "Dear combatants, soldiers of the Croatian Defence Council, commanders and deputy commanders, officers and non-commissioned officers, the Croatian people, and numerous local representatives of Zenica city council and Zenica municipality, on behalf of the Croatian Defence Council Main Staff, chief of Central Bosnia Operation, I congratulate you sincerely on being sworn in today. "Thank you. "This is definitely a historic day for the Jure Francetic Brigade, but let me emphasise that the actual historic day for us occurred much earlier than today, when the Croatian people and the municipality of Zenica understood that the time had come to take up arms to defend their right to exist in their own land. You, my dear brethren, took this oath on the 13th of August and much earlier, when you went on your first and most difficult mission to assist the defenders of the city of Jajce, and when 460 of you left these parts to defend those Croatian territories, and not just Jajce but also Zepce and all the territories where the command told you to go. Today's ceremony is, therefore, definitely a historic event, yet another in a string of events most relevant to the growth and creation of the Croatian Defence Council, the Croatian People's Army."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, we've heard a few references now to the homeland being Herceg-Bosna, and now Tihomir Blaskic talking about the Croatian Defence Council as the Croatian People's Army. Now, this is December of 1992, so there's already been a conflict in Prozor by this time, but what we're seeing here, General, is the establishment of essentially a purely Croatian military unit whose function is to protect Herceg-Bosna, without regard to really anything beyond Herceg-Bosna such as the broader Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that true? This was a Croatian army for a Croatian homeland and only that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. Here -- well, if you heard mention of Jure Francetic as a fight on the Salonika front, which dates back to the First World War, where the Serbs were fighting, the Serbs were fighting there on the side of the victors in World War I, and Jure Francetic at the time was a fighter at the Salonika front, and these are famous facts and the famous history of the Serb people. Secondly, here reference is made to citizens. It specifically says "citizens." And then, furthermore, there was mobilisation, and of course there is always death involved in the realisation of national rights. There was a delegation from Zenica here, not only from the Croatian people. Now, I don't know whether there were any Muslims in the unit, but mention is made of that, too. So taking all of this into account, if we look and see -- if we look at the beginnings of the bloody war, rather the Serb take-over, this kind of rhetoric is allowed, and it has nothing in it that could be taken as being invalid or something that is not in order. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] Let me just say that I did not mention -- that I did not note that these words that Mr. Praljak mentioned now were translated in the original text, the words that the delegation of the municipality of the town of Zenica. I did not note that word, "delegation," in the English language, and since Mr. Praljak mentioned that now, I'd like to intervene because of the translation and the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's very important, and I'd like it to be added that Herceg-Bosna is always mentioned in two forms, and that is throughout history Herceg-Bosna was equated and was identical to Bosnia-Herzegovina. And in Franjo Tudjman's books, the ones we skipped through, he speaks about -- when he speaks of Herceg-Bosna, he speaks of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the term used at a given period of history. So Herceg-Bosna, mentioned in the historical context, is Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's the name we gave to Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's how we called Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, the second part is this other Herceg-Bosna with all the connotations that we've discussed again and again and has the different organisational connotations as having emerged from this war, the latest war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, Mr. Prlic said something. He knows English very well, so nothing escapes him. He said that they were representatives of the municipality of Zenica during this swearing-in ceremony, and this is not in the English text. Now, given the fact that there were representatives of the municipality of Zenica, does this mean that there were Muslims present during this event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Judge Antonetti, Your Honour. And if you might allow me to take just a minute of the Court's time to explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. You're telling us that Muslims were present. When people are singing the Croatian anthem, because in answering a question put to you by Mr. Stringer you did say that this was the Croatian anthem, well, these Muslims who were present, what do they feel? Do they think it's natural, do they feel that this is natural, or is this an interference with the regular anthem of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time did not have its own national anthem. Unfortunately, it still hasn't got an anthem, and today's anthem was written by someone from the international community or something like that. Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time had no national anthem, so this is the national anthem of the Croatian people. It wasn't the national anthem of goodness knows what. And to be frank, it doesn't speak about any war or anything like that. It's a very mild text, and it is also the anthem of the Croatian state in Croatia, but it's much more than that. It's the national anthem of the Croatian people which is sung today as well, quite normally at many festivals and festivities, as a second hymn within Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Bosnia-Herzegovinian anthem is played and then it's the national anthem that is played -- or, actually, it's not a national anthem; it's an anthem because there is no state to proclaim it a national anthem. But Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time did not have either an official song of any kind or a national anthem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you've understood, of course, that for the Prosecutor this is incriminating evidence, but you're saying that at the time there was no official anthem. Is that what you're saying? That's your answer to his question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then we saw a second group, a band with a guitar, and people are singing. What are they singing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know now. Perhaps we should play it again. I don't know what they were singing when this guitar was going. It was still the national anthem, they were still playing the national anthem; right? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, it's another thing, just a song. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know now.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Just a correction for the transcript, but I can wait. I'll take my turn after you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll refrain from saying "ladies first," because it would not be fitting, I think. I would just like to point out that in one of the addresses given at the beginning, the speaker speaks of representatives of Zenica city and Zenica municipality, so it's not true that this does not figure in the transcript. Also, the deputy chief of Zenica, sort of, is mentioned in the beginning. So I think that there has been an oversight, perhaps. Excuse me. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: I didn't see that. I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It can happen, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to make another correction to the transcript. On page 76, lines 8 and 9, linked to the oath that was taken by the soldiers, the general said that the reference in the oath was to citizens. In the transcript, this was translated as "citizens," "gradjani," "citizens." I would like to remind the Trial Chamber of our discussions with counsel. Buntic, who was Dr. Prlic's witness, and I think that at the time we cleared up the difference between these concepts in the Croatian language. In Croatian, you have the word "gradjani," which is translated by the word "residents," and "drzavljani," which is translated as "citizens." Now, the difference in these two terms is essential, because the word here used is "gradjani."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And counsel says that is "residents," interpreters note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, it refers to all the people in the territory. Everybody will be defended. The word "gradjani."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, "citizens."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not the Croats who are going to be defended, it is the "gradjani" who are going to be defended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm listening to the English channel, and I think there is some disagreement between what's being said here in the courtroom and what's coming from the interpretation booth on the English translation of the word, but beyond that I'm not going to make any more comments because I doubt that it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, something you said earlier that I want to challenge you on. Are you claiming that when they say "Herceg-Bosna" here, what they really mean is "Bosnia-Herzegovina"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, I would have to listen to the tape, but in historical documents and in documents generally, Franjo Tudjman's books that we went through so quickly, so rapidly, very often what happens is this: The concept "Herceg-Bosna" coincides with the concept of "Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to -- I'm going to put it to you that if you're suggesting that Herceg-Bosna, as it's being used here, is a reference to the entirety of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is an evasion on your part, it's not accurate, and it's really not based on anything that we've seen or heard previously in this entire trial. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I told you precisely what I meant. I would have to listen to the tape again because I can't say what the man was thinking of, but I'm just saying historically speaking, historical documents, even Franjo Tudjman's documents, and I can quote you pages from his books, in a paragraph he might say "Herceg-Bosna," and in another paragraph he might say "Bosnia-Herzegovina," meaning the same state territory. So these are two concepts which in literature and in speech were very often interchangeable. They had the same -- they meant the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, when Tihomir Blaskic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, just a small detail in passing, an ancillary question. Earlier we saw Mr. Kordic. I watched him closely, and I noted that he was dressed in a uniform, in a military uniform. He had a military uniform on. Mr. Kordic was an elected official from the municipality. Does this mean that at the time there was a bit of a confusion between the two roles, that you could be a civilian and military and there was no difference between the two? Otherwise, how could you explain that Mr. Kordic would be dressed in a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A point of order. Could we see that passage again, because according to my recollection it was a gentleman standing slightly behind the military, in civil clothes, and so we have looked at the same but seen different things, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please take a look at the frame?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, I think there won't be any disagreement. If we look at the frame that's on the screen now, we have the speaker in the middle, at the microphone, and then behind him on the left, wearing the sunglasses, is Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I was right. Thank you. This is Kordic. He's got sunglasses and he's wearing a military uniform. Can you say, "Da," so that it's recorded, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why is he wearing this military uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Because he held a rank. I can explain this precisely, because I participated in all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why does he have a rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because in 1992 the Serbs kept asking for negotiations about Sarajevo and in Sarajevo, et cetera. Tihomir Blaskic went to such negotiations. It lasted for days. Honestly speaking, we all knew it would lead to nothing. At the same time, he could not work on the organisation of the Croatian Defence Council. I asked Mate Boban, Your Honours, to assign a rank to Kordic. Otherwise, the Serbs would not have accepted him as a negotiator. For him to go there and waste his time during those false negotiations, I wanted Blaskic to dedicate himself to our defence. Boban listened to me and Kordic was given a rank. Otherwise, he would not have been accepted as a collocutor at those lengthy negotiations. And Blaskic could then dedicate himself to our defence. That's the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We can go back to it, but I would point out for the record, at the beginning of the transcript which everyone, I believe, has in their binders, the speaker introduces Dario Kordic as the Herceg-Bosna vice-president. And in addition, and the general was present, and he can correct me if I'm wrong, but the other civilian persons who are introduced there are within the structure of the HVO or HDZ, as opposed to a different governmental structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to explain how it came about that I was there. I wasn't very familiar with the whole procedure. I'll do so, with your leave. I know for sure that there were Muslim representatives from Zenica there. I can explain to you how it was that I came there to this gathering.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just for the record, you're saying there were Muslim representatives present. Are you saying that there were Muslim representatives who were present who were on the stage there behind the speaker or were they somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say with any certainty whether they were on the stage, but I remember some discussion about the Muslims being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, why don't we continue with the video, then.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "It started with the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was the first to find its way in these difficult times ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is - I don't think it's in dispute - Ignjac Kostroman. The Trial Chamber knows what his position was in the HZ-HB or the HVO, so I'm -- we all have the transcript. I'm proposing to skip over him. We could just advance a little more quickly, at least, without losing our place, to the next speaker. Okay. And then this is the priest speaking, and I believe when we saw this video earlier Judge Antonetti asked you whether HVO units had priests or chaplains among their ranks, and I believe you testified that they did not, so I'm going to skip over the remarks of the priest here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just one question on this, General. Did you consider it inappropriate that a priest was addressing the unit at the swearing-in ceremony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that to be inappropriate. There was no reason to, in such conditions when the state was falling apart and people were defending their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So if we can continue, then, skipping along. Now, Mr. President, this is, I believe, Dominik Sakic who was a local HDZ or HVO person. I'm proposing to skip over his speech. And then we'll get to your speech, General.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Soldiers, NCOs, COs, congratulations on your oath to your people. We've applauded you. Please don't smoke during the celebration. Put our your cigarettes. Gentlemen, the idea of the people is a great idea, and it isn't as cold as it seems. Twenty-five minutes is not too long. We can stand 25 minutes in file without smoking a cigarette. Keep in mind that there are many nations older than us, more numerous than us, not greater than us but more numerous, who do not have their own state. You can't set up a state so easily. Every day, you have to devote yourself to your people's idea of a state. The state is not a mother, it is a child to be nursed and helped by each of us and not taken advantage of. Keep defence in mind when you start digging, when you guard your weapons, when you walk in the street, and in every other situation. The idea of the Croatian people will exist in these territories depending on our willingness to devote ourselves to this idea. Merry Christmas, Happy New Year, bless you and good luck. Remember your friends who are no longer with us. It will give you strength in difficult times. Good luck and God bless you. Thank you."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, you're addressing a unit that's been referred to by its direct commander, General Blaskic, as the Croatian People's Army. Here you speak and you use on two occasions the notion of a state, you say you can't set up a state so easily, every day you have to devote yourself to your people's idea of a state. Now, isn't it true, General, that the state you're referring to, the entity that you're referring to, is not the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but rather you're referring to an autonomous Croatian area that we've been talking about today, whether it is named Herceg-Bosna or whether it has a different name? Isn't that the state that you're referring to here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Zenica, for me in Zenica to say that we were there to create a Croatian state, no, sir. My speech is crystal clear. I stand by every word of it today, about what I said, that they shouldn't smoke. I stand by each and every word. I wouldn't change a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if a major general of the Croatian Army, who's also a member of the National Defence Council of the Republic of Croatia, is addressing a unit such as this in Zenica and speaks of a state, that could be viewed as highly provocative, couldn't it, by persons who were not members of this unit or who do not wish to associate themselves with the Croatian state?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, people can do lots of things, but we are speaking here about a rational human mind, from that perspective, I am a citizen -- a national of Bosnia-Herzegovina who was born and raised there in Zenica, where there weren't all that many Croats. And before that, I participated in the defence of Travnik after Jajce had fallen, in joint combat. I stand by every word of mine. Only in complete malice one could find anything here that would be against --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, the question of the Prosecutor was very important. He presents to us the document, which we have already seen. Remember, I had asked you a question about the boy who holds the flag, and I had asked you whether, in the Croatian Army, there were young, minor boys, so I remember very well this video. Now, this question of the Prosecutor is very important. You're making a speech, and in this speech you are speaking about the creation of a state. The question is the following, therefore: Do you refer to the state of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or are you referring to the state of the Herceg-Bosna, this under oath? Can you answer understand oath? To which state are you referring when you're uttering these words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the umpteenth time, and giving any oath, I would still repeat the same, I had in mind the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In Zenica, by that time there were 80 per cent Muslims, and the HVO was establishing a unit there to fight for Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was not the flag of the Republic of Croatia, but the flag of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. These units were there to defend Zenica and that area from the Serb aggressor. What was meant was exclusively Bosnia-Herzegovina. The issue of the way Bosnia-Herzegovina would be structured and set up is another matter. These two questions are being mixed up here. Yes, Bosnia-Herzegovina, but such a Bosnia and Herzegovina in which the Croatian people would be on an equal footing with the two other peoples in a sustainable mode of survival. Any state which would prejudice that would have been unacceptable, and this we see happening today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Do you know whether Bosnia and Herzegovina had a national anthem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bosnia and Herzegovina did have -- no, Judge Trechsel, Bosnia and Herzegovina did not have an anthem. There was the Yugoslav anthem, and within Yugoslavia, as far as I know, only Croats had their national anthem, and I think Slovenians who sometimes sang their anthem. The Serb anthem, "Boze Pravde," was not allowed in Yugoslavia. The Croatian one was only permitted at 12.00 news. Then "Lijepa Nasa" was played. Otherwise, only "Hej Slaveni," the Yugoslav anthem, was played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to move on now. The next speaker, General, although I don't think we need to listen to his speech, is Ante Prkacin, and we have the text. I don't think we need to listen to his speech. It's about Jure Francetic. And then after that, we get to Dario Kordic, and I did want to play the Dario Kordic part.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Dear Croatian brethren, dear Croatian soldiers, I greet you on behalf of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and on behalf of the greatest son of the Croatian people of Herceg-Bosna, the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Mate Boban. You heard about messages these days. They tell us why we are fighting for liberation and a political solution for the Croatian people. This is because we don't want, ever again, to repeat the mistakes that we kept making in the past. So, from this place today, at this ceremony made by the Croatian Defence Council, Jure Francetic Brigade, the Croatian soldiers show that they are as brave as the people before them and the people before me said, and will certainly fulfill our mission with all our heart and soul, the mission laid before us by generations of Croatian soldiers from centuries ago, and by our families and children, who definitely deserve a better future. In the name of that, long live the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, long live everyone. Merry Christmas and happy holidays. At the ready for the homeland. "At the ready."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, just getting to the first few lines of this speech, General, he's greeting the soldiers on behalf of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and on behalf of the greatest son of the Croatian people of Herceg-Bosna, Mate Boban. Now, the fact is that all the references in this -- in these various speeches to Herceg-Bosna are references to just that, Herceg-Bosna, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and not Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to find a better position, since my back aches. The point is that Dario Kordic was a very strong-worded politician, which is natural in times such as these. One cannot use philosophical concepts to induce people to go and fight and perhaps be killed. Dario Kordic was talking about a political solution and liberation. He was referring to the liberation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if you heard it, but within the framework of that liberation we need such a political situation in which Croatians would no longer be suppressed. This is what's in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question. My question is this: Do you agree with me that all the references here to Herceg-Bosna are references just to that, Herceg-Bosna, and that this isn't intended as any sort of reference to Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is what you were suggesting earlier? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know whether he meant Herceg-Bosna as Bosnia-Herzegovina or Herceg-Bosna as a project which was supposed to liberate Bosnia and Herzegovina and enable its survival. What Dario Kordic had in mind at that time, I don't know, but "Herceg-Bosna" was used in two ways, both as a temporary unit for the Croatian people, until a resolution is found for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and as a synonym for Bosnia-Herzegovina. In any case, Dario Kordic mentions the political solution and liberation. One could say that when he says "Herceg-Bosna," he means "Bosnia and Herzegovina." He says the liberation of the country within which preconditions favourable to Croats were needed. This is what I heard, and you can perhaps play it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General, I mean, I don't know why you'd want to defend Dario Kordic. I'm going to suggest to you it's clear that Dario Kordic had no interest whatsoever in any political solutions other than autonomy and separation from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We both know that to be true, don't we?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Perhaps you're more knowledgeable than me. I don't see what you're saying. It's not in any documents. And as for what Dario Kordic meant will always remain unclear. What I read from this is liberation and political solution. "Liberation" refers to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the politician solution pertains to the status of the Croatian people within such a Bosnia-Herzegovina. As far as I know him, he was quite loyal to the general political position and its implementation. I don't know any more than that. Dario Kordic had to abide by the conclusions and positions signed by the authorised officials who represented the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right, General. Well, at the very end, and this is going to be my last question on this videotape, at the very end we don't get it through the interpretation into English, probably not into French, but I understand that in the language he's speaking, the Serbo-Croatian, Kordic says the words at the very end "za dom," and all of the soldiers respond, "Spremni." Now, isn't it true, sir, that that's a Ustasha greeting or statement, if you will, from the World War II era, it's also a very highly provocative one, especially to be using in Zenica in December of 1992; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with you that there is such a language as Serbo-Croatian. What Dario Kordic said was in Croatian, and that is one of the reasons for the war, because it was generally thought that small nations should not divide such things as languages, and it resulted in such things we witnessed. Those at the bottom of the food-chain do not enjoy the same dignity as those at the top. And as for "za dom, spremni," it was used by both the Ustasha and "domobrani." In the Croatian military practice, however, historically speaking, it had been used even before that. Therefore, whether in this context it implied the NDH greeting or was this a reference to some earlier Croatian uprising -- uprises which took place in, say, Lika, well, I don't want to speculate on that. In any case, if I may have another moment, I wanted to refer to Kraljevic and who had letter U and the black Ustasha uniform, and then everyone who came from abroad said, "Look, all Croats are Ustashas." This was a disaster because the Croatian people did away with that a long time before that. This was a highly-sensitive issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Unless there are more questions on the video, Mr. President, I'm ready to move to the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a technical question. We see on the screen, on the monitor, this flag. There are three colours, red, white and blue, and one can see the chess-board on the white. At the period of the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, did you have the chess-board?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the days of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the flag was red, white and blue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So which one was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The three colours intermingled, but in different order. The Serb one was in one order, then the other republics had the other order. The three colours were there as from the times of the French Revolution. In any case, there were the three colours in different order, the white, red and blue, with the five-pointed star in the middle. In Croatia, historically speaking, the Croatian flag and coat of arms were tolerated. However, this is not the coat of arms of the Republic of Croatia. This is the historical Croatian coat of arm. The state coat of arm of Croatia does not look like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A final question. You told us that there were Muslim representatives. Why were they not given the floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what I wanted to explain, Your Honours. I came to this meeting because Prkacin asked me to go to the Zenica prison, where he wanted to intervene for someone, and I was his driver, in actual fact, while he was negotiating in there, so I was acting as a driver, and I was talking to the people there that way. He went to the municipality to talk to the Muslims, to see what this man had done wrong and so on, and that's where we were invited to the meeting from. And I'm not ashamed. I told them what I said and I told them what I wanted to tell them, but as I say, I wasn't informed -- well, I saw the Muslims, I saw that. Now, why they weren't given the floor, why they weren't given a chance to speak, I don't know, and I didn't take part in any of the preparations for the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... being organised by whom? Who had decided that this ceremony would take place; Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The HVO. Yes, Blaskic, correct. And this unit was established in Zenica, and he was the organiser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next document in the binder should be Exhibit 3D00482. You testified about this document already on the 7th of May. 3D00482. These are minutes made of a meeting that took place on the 15th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 13th was the meeting, the 13th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I stand corrected. The 13th was the date of the meeting, and then the minutes here that we're looking at are dated two days later on the 15th of January. These are talks in which you participated with General Quesnot, who was the chief of the staff of the Presidency of the Republic of France, according to this document, and as you've indicated, the meeting itself was held on the 13th of January. And I want to direct your attention to some of the remarks that you made. First, I'm just noting on the first page, on the second paragraph, it's indicated here that at this meeting you appeared in your capacity as a major general and assistant minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia, and you were there with other high-level individuals in the military of the Croatian Army. Turning to the next page, I'm going to take you to the paragraph that begins with the words: "According to General Praljak's opinion, such situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina is going to last for a long period of time." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you talk about the Serbs, the Serbian leadership and the promises they've made to their people, and then you say: "As far as the Muslims are concerned, a common -- actually, a Muslim state has been promised. They had many dead people within the ethnic cleansing, and now they are trying to capitalise their victim. The Croatian position has been clear from the very beginning. The territory that belongs to the Croats matches the borders of the Banovina Hrvatska from 1933 division of Yugoslavia, synchronised with the 1981 census. The 1991 census is not valid. The Croats stand for Bosnia and Herzegovina as integrity, as state, as well as the rights of Croats as constitutive nation. The problems among the Croats and Muslims are results of variety of goals within the political fights. The Croats fight for the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, with autonomy for the Croats, while the Muslims fight for the civil state." Now, just to take the second part of this first, General, I'm going to suggest to you that what you're saying here is consistent with what you've said on several occasions throughout your testimony, that the autonomy for Croats is an objective of the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They want autonomy. They do not want to exist within a civil or unitary state in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Completely correct. I never agreed, and don't today, no matter your threats, that I be a part of a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina which denies the existence of a nation to which I belonged. So what I said there I consign today as being fully true. So the Banovina just refers to the part in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but in conformity with the population census it can be smaller. The Muslims want their majority and their own state, the Serbs want 80 per cent of the territory, and the Croats want what they have a right to under the Constitution and according to their rights, a form of autonomy on the territory where they represent the absolute majority or vast majority, of course, with all the other people living in the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And today, too, I consign this and subscribe to it fully. I think it is politically correct, reasonable, and I have nothing more to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let me suggest to you, General, that there's been a slight modification or variance between what you've just said and what's reported or ascribed to you in this document. What you're saying -- what you said in this document is that the territory, that autonomous area that belongs to the Croats here, matches the borders of the Banovina Hrvatska, so what you're saying here is two things. There's going to be an autonomous Croatian territory, and that in fact that territory is going to be the equivalent of the territory that was the banovina within Bosnia-Herzegovina. Isn't that clearly what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it coincides with the borders, of course, of the Banovina of Croatia from the Yugoslav division, the part that refers to Bosnia-Herzegovina, of course, and it says dovetailed with the 1981 population census, which means less than the Banovina, because we'd already lost a percentage of the population there, Mr. Prosecutor. So it means synchronised or dovetailed, so we're even less than the Banovina, where we were in a lesser position than we were in 1939, and it says the Croats are striving for an integral Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state, and the rights of the Croats as a constitutive nation, and then it goes on to explain the problems. And I say this to the largest French delegation. This is crystal clear, and that is the policy and the politics that I am advocating here on behalf of -- well, that was Croatia's policy, and Tudjman's, and Jadranko Prlic's, and all of us. The constituent element are the Croats, so don't confuse us with the Muslims, or the Serbs, or the embargoes enforced, and this is just crystal clear, as clear as can be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Please calm down, Mr. Praljak, calm down, and we may finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 7.00 p.m. We have to finish now. We will continue tomorrow. We have important questions to ask on the basis of the documents. We will discuss these matters. As you know, tomorrow we will be sitting in the morning, so we will meet in a few hours for a hearing which will start at 9.00 a.m. Therefore, I wish everybody a pleasant evening, and we'll meet again tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
